finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so the 'dba' role check is never enforced. Any caller who reaches the handler can run DROP TABLE.
finding.source: Any HTTP client hitting /admin/drop. Authentication is only needed to populate the user in the context, and no role is needed. The table name comes from the attacker-controlled form value 't'.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27, a destructive DDL operation

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered to dropTable with no auth middleware
userFrom(r) gets the user from the context
Authorize(u, "dba") returns the error "forbidden" for non-dba users, but the return value is discarded and execution continues

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is the Authorize call at line 26, and its result is not checked. vacuum (api.go:33-36) checks the error correctly, which shows the check was intended here. No middleware wraps the handler (api.go:44). There is no HTTP method restriction.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the bare-statement call discards it. userFrom (api.go:22) panics if no user is in the context, so the caller must be authenticated by something outside this file. No other check, middleware, or table-name allowlist exists.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards Authorize's "forbidden" error (api.go:19), so api.go:27 runs DROP TABLE with the unsanitized form value "t" for any user who gets a *User into the context. The vacuum handler at api.go:33-36 shows the correct pattern. The only caveat is that anonymous callers would hit a panic at api.go:22, so the attacker must be any authenticated low-privilege user.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded as a bare statement. No middleware wraps the handler at api.go:44, and no method restriction exists.
verdict_facts.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize, so any authenticated user, regardless of role, reaches runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27. This is unlike vacuum, which checks the error at api.go:33.

finding.claim: SQL injection in DDL: the table name from r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into the statement with no validation or identifier quoting. Even a legitimate dba can inject arbitrary SQL (for example `x; DROP DATABASE ...` or stacked statements), and combined with F1 any user can.
finding.source: Form or query parameter 't', controlled by the caller. FormValue reads both the URL query and the POST body, so a plain GET also works.

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") is concatenated directly into the SQL string
runSQL is a stub, but its signature takes a raw string, so there is no parameterisation or allowlist

finding.guards_checked: There is no allowlist of table names, no identifier quoting or regexp validation, and no HTTP method check. Authorization is bypassed per F1. DDL identifiers cannot be bound as parameters, so only validation or quoting would help.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded, so it is not enforced. There is no allowlist, quoting or validation of "t", and no method check.
verdict.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into "DROP TABLE " with no validation, and the only guard at api.go:26 discards Authorize's error, so any authenticated user can inject. The stacked-statement impact depends on the real runSQL driver, which is a stub at api.go:41.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 returns an error, but the result is discarded, so it blocks nothing. There is no allowlist, quoting or validation of "t", and no method check.
verdict_facts.reason: api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into the DROP TABLE statement with no validation or quoting. The only guard, Authorize at api.go:26, has its error ignored, so any user can inject SQL beyond the DROP TABLE a dba would be allowed to run.

finding.claim: userFrom does an unchecked type assertion on the context value. If no authentication middleware has set "user", or the value has a different type, the assertion panics. net/http recovers the panic per request, so this is a low-severity denial of service or fail-open risk, depending on how the missing middleware is eventually wired in. The string context key is also collision-prone.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated request reaching /admin/* when no middleware populates the context

trace.note: The routes are registered without any wrapping auth middleware
The single-value type assertion panics on a nil interface

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware exists in this file. There is no comma-ok assertion and no nil check. net/http recovers panics per connection, so the process stays up.

verdict.guard_found: none (no middleware, no comma-ok assertion, no nil check; only net/http's per-request panic recovery)
verdict.reason: api.go:22 does an unchecked `.(*User)` assertion and api.go:44-45 register the routes with no middleware that sets "user", so any anonymous request to /admin/* panics. net/http recovers it per request, so the impact is low severity, and the handlers currently fail closed because the panic happens before runSQL at api.go:27 and api.go:37.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Trusted upstream middleware populates the request identity (per project facts), so the "user" context value is set before handlers run. net/http also recovers handler panics per request.
verdict_facts.reason: The api.go:22 assertion and the route registration at api.go:44 are as described, but the finding depends on no middleware setting "user", and the project facts say trusted upstream middleware always populates it. Without that premise the only outcome is a per-request recovered panic, which is not a vulnerability. The separate bug at api.go:26, where dropTable discards Authorize's result, is a different finding.
